title: Classical polynomial-time algorithms for cryptographic lattice problems

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a classical algorithm that solves cryptographically relevant lattice problems in polynomial time, with resource costs low enough to attack real cryptographic parameters. A lattice is a regular collection of points generated by integer combinations of basis vectors. The shortest-vector problem asks for its shortest nonzero vector. Search Learning with Errors, or search LWE, asks for secret variables hidden in random linear equations perturbed by small errors. Those errors make ordinary linear equation solving insufficient. ML-KEM, the standardized key-encapsulation mechanism, relies on a structured variant called Module Learning with Errors, or Module-LWE.

The intended capability would overcome the trade-off between fast lattice reduction and sufficiently accurate solutions. Polynomial-time LLL reduction provides an approximation guarantee that grows exponentially with dimension. Stronger reduction and search methods can obtain better solutions at much greater computational cost. The innovation requires a method that reaches the problem distributions and solution quality relevant to cryptography while retaining polynomial scaling.

Scope synthesis: a compelling practical target is recovery of ML-KEM-1024 shared secrets from public encapsulation keys and ciphertexts. Success against that target would establish a consequential cryptanalytic capability, but its mathematical breadth would depend on the algorithm. An attack exploiting the structure of Module-LWE could be narrower than a general lattice algorithm. An implementation vulnerability would demonstrate a different capability. The proposed innovation has not been established by the supplied evidence.

significance.text: NIST standardized ML-KEM as an alternative to key-establishment schemes based on integer factorization and discrete logarithms, which are vulnerable to sufficiently capable quantum computers. At publication in 2024, NIST described ML-KEM as believed secure even against quantum adversaries. A practical classical algorithm solving the actual search instances underlying ML-KEM would undermine that distinct security assumption and enable recovery of encryption secrets and encapsulated shared keys from public information.

The practical consequence would depend on total attack cost, including constants, memory, and preprocessing, as well as the polynomial degree. If those costs were manageable, a mechanism designed for post-quantum key establishment could become vulnerable on classical computers. Previously recorded communications could also become readable when the necessary encapsulation transcript is available, confidentiality depends on the recovered shared secret, and no independent protocol protection survives. Recovering one cryptographic secret does not automatically defeat every protocol that incorporates it.

Impact synthesis: this would be a major advance in mathematics and cryptanalysis because it would turn a presumed computational barrier into an efficient constructive procedure. Its consequences would extend to lattice signatures, fully homomorphic encryption, and other lattice constructions only where the attack also defeats their particular problems, distributions, and parameters. A general shortest-vector algorithm would threaten ML-KEM only through an applicable reduction or explicit attack connecting its approximation guarantee and running time to the scheme; a worst-case hardness reduction cannot simply be read backward as an attack. Developing secure replacements would remain a separate undertaking.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability is efficient classical recovery of cryptographic secrets at the dimensions, noise levels, moduli, and algebraic structure used by the target schemes. The documented algorithmic obstacle is the time-versus-quality trade-off in lattice reduction and search: LLL is polynomial-time with an exponential approximation guarantee, sieving is described as exponential-time, and BKZ trades computational effort against reduction quality. These observations concern known algorithms; they are not a proof that every possible algorithm must take exponential time.

For an ML-KEM attack, the mathematical bridge must reach the scheme's actual Module-LWE instances. A solution for a different noise distribution, specially chosen secret, altered modulus, or easier parameter range would not automatically transfer. Likewise, a decision procedure that distinguishes distributions, or a general lattice approximation theorem, needs a demonstrated route to the secret-recovery or shared-key-recovery objective. FIPS 203 provides the concrete computational assumption and encapsulation structure against which that route must be assessed.

Engineering synthesis: the method must remain feasible after accounting for data requirements, preprocessing, memory, arithmetic precision, and success probability. A polynomial expression with an enormous exponent or constants could establish an asymptotic advance without making standardized parameters practically vulnerable. Conversely, an effective attack on one fixed parameter set could be a serious security break without establishing polynomial-time scaling. The proposed innovation requires both a justified scaling claim and a meaningful practical demonstration.

current_state.text: NIST published FIPS 203 on August 13, 2024, approving ML-KEM-512, ML-KEM-768, and ML-KEM-1024. The standard identifies ML-KEM-1024 with security category 5 and bases ML-KEM's security on presumed Module-LWE hardness. It also attributes the introduction of LWE to Regev in 2005. These are documented developments in cryptographic construction and standardization, rather than demonstrations of a polynomial-time attack or proofs of computational hardness. NIST's statement of security against quantum adversaries expresses its belief at publication.

Alice Pellet-Mary's June 20, 2024 lecture documents polynomial-time LLL reduction with an exponential approximation guarantee, exponential-time sieving, and BKZ trade-offs. It describes sufficiently demanding lattice approximation problems as having no known polynomial-time solution, including in the quantum setting. The supplied review supports that qualitative account, but not a comprehensive claim about the best attack in every cryptographic LWE regime. Exponent formatting in the extracted LLL summary is imperfect, and the extracted BKZ graph does not support precise numerical cryptographic thresholds.

A MathOverflow answer dated April 19, 2024 reproduces Yilei Chen's April 18 update concerning ePrint 2024/555. The update reports a bug in step 9 and withdraws the claim of a polynomial-time quantum algorithm for LWE with polynomial modulus-noise ratios. This is the documented scope of the invalidated claim; it should not be replaced by the different condition of polynomial modulus alone. The evidence is a reproduced author update in a discussion page, not an independent assessment of the original manuscript, and it does not establish that the entire paper was formally retracted.

Evidence limitation: the supplied material does not substantiate the earlier survey claim that machine-learning attacks recover only weakened or small sparse-secret instances, nor does it establish the absence of a practical ML-KEM-1024 attack through November 1, 2026. The supplied freshness search record is empty. The justified conclusion is that these materials do not establish the proposed breakthrough; they also do not prove that no later breakthrough exists. Correct exhaustive or exponential algorithms must be distinguished from attacks that are computationally feasible.

The supplied review reports that the retained FIPS 203 extraction is truncated at the end of Appendix C. The passages supporting the standard's publication date, computational assumption, parameter sets, and relevant encapsulation operations are intact. That limitation does not undermine those specific statements, but the supplied extraction should not be treated as a complete inspection of every part of the standard.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed mathematical demonstration: publish a refereed classical algorithm with a correctness argument and an explicit polynomial running-time bound for a clearly defined, growing family of cryptographically relevant instances. State the input representation, parameter relationships, success probability, and whether the guarantee is worst-case or distributional. Include all preprocessing and resource costs. These are proposed criteria for making the innovation convincing, not established certification standards.
completion_criteria.label: Refereed classical algorithm proves correctness and polynomial running time

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical demonstration: reproducibly recover shared secrets from public encapsulation keys and ciphertexts at the unmodified ML-KEM-1024 parameter set, using independently generated keys and encapsulations. FIPS 203 supplies the definition of this target and its public inputs; it does not prescribe this proposed test. The experiment should measure success across multiple independent instances, rather than relying on one successful recovery.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible shared-secret recovery across multiple independent unmodified ML-KEM-1024 instances

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirements: release the algorithm, implementation, instance-generation procedure, and sufficient experimental records for independent replication on documented classical hardware. Report elapsed time, memory, preprocessing, sample requirements, failures, and any amortization across targets. The attack should use no private keys, secret randomness, implementation leakage, or specially weakened instances. A modest BKZ improvement or a toy-parameter attack would not meet this proposed demonstration unless it also establishes the required capability.
completion_criteria.label: Release reproducible public-input-only classical attack with full resource accounting

completion_criteria.text: Proposed interpretation boundaries: experiments at ML-KEM-1024 would demonstrate performance at that parameter set, while the complexity argument would establish the claimed asymptotic scaling. Finite tests establish demonstrated breadth, not literal universality. A Module-LWE-specific result should state that scope explicitly; claims about general shortest-vector problems or other cryptographic constructions need their own arguments and demonstrations. An invalidated quantum claim cannot satisfy a classical-algorithm criterion.
completion_criteria.label: Distinguish ML-KEM-1024 performance from asymptotic scaling and broader claims

related_concepts.text: MAT-06, Classical polynomial-time integer factorization and discrete logarithms, is a sibling cryptographic breakthrough with a different mathematical target. FIPS 203 explicitly distinguishes ML-KEM's presumed Module-LWE hardness from factorization- and discrete-logarithm-based key establishment. An algorithm for either target does not automatically provide an algorithm for the other. This comparison concerns the supplied MAT-06 title and that documented distinction; no fuller MAT-06 record was supplied.

Relationship synthesis: MAT-01, Practical polynomial-time algorithms for NP-complete problems, has potentially broader implications. The earlier reasoning that such an advance would not affect lattice problems because they are not known to be NP-complete is insufficient. A general practical solver for NP-complete problems could, through suitable encodings and search reductions, solve polynomially verifiable bounded-witness tasks without those tasks themselves being NP-complete. Whether this produces a practical lattice attack depends on the formulation, encoding overhead, and algorithm's costs. A specialized lattice breakthrough would not by itself establish a general solver for NP-complete problems.

Relationship synthesis: MAT-02, An effective global Langlands correspondence over number fields, concerns a different arithmetic capability; no supplied argument connects it directly to efficient lattice cryptanalysis. MAT-05, Research-scale machine-checked mathematical discovery, could help develop or verify an algorithm and its proof, but is a discovery and verification capability rather than the lattice-solving result itself. MAT-07, A prescriptive mathematical theory of deep learning, could inform learning-based attack methods, but does not establish that those methods solve cryptographic lattice instances.

Relationship synthesis: MAT-03, A first-principles theory of turbulent transport; MAT-04, Proved polynomial-cost solution of high-dimensional nonlinear PDEs; and MAT-08, Polynomial-time chemical accuracy for molecular electronic structure, share the ambition of overcoming difficult computational or predictive barriers. Their target problems, accuracy requirements, and mathematical structures differ from lattice secret recovery. The supplied roster provides no reduction or demonstrated algorithmic implication linking those capabilities to MAT-09. Each remains a separate innovation.

unresolved_issues: Whether a later practical classical or quantum breakthrough occurred by November 1, 2026 remains unresolved because the supplied freshness search record is empty.
The claimed scope and limitations of machine-learning attacks on sparse-secret instances require a supported attack survey.
The original Ajtai historical attribution is not established by the retained reviewed sources.
Precise approximation thresholds connecting a proposed general lattice algorithm to ML-KEM require an applicable reduction or explicit attack; the extracted BKZ figure does not resolve them.
Chen's original manuscript and subsequent revisions were not independently inspected in the supplied review, so only the reproduced April 18, 2024 withdrawal is established here.

No specific polynomial degree, resource budget, or experimental success threshold has been established as sufficient for practical completion; these require explicit justification for a proposed algorithm.

brief.title: Fast solutions to the maths protecting encryption
possible: Ordinary computers could recover encryption secrets from public information by efficiently solving lattice problems, mathematical puzzles about regular grids of points. A concrete target is ML-KEM-1024, a standard method for establishing a shared secret key.

The algorithm would run in polynomial time, meaning its running time grows as a fixed power of problem size. Its total computing costs would also be low enough to attack the settings used in real cryptography.
why: Organisations using ML-KEM to protect communications against future quantum computers would face an attack from ordinary computers. An efficient mathematical solution would overturn the security assumption behind that protection.

sources.who: National Institute of Standards and Technology
sources.showed: NIST standardized ML-KEM for establishing shared secret keys. Its security rests on the presumed difficulty of solving equations with deliberately added small errors.
sources.cited_for: The standard defines the cryptographic target and the public information an attack would use.
sources.not_established: Standardization supplies neither a proof of computational hardness nor an efficient attack.

sources.showed: Pellet-Mary reviewed algorithms for lattice problems. Fast methods give limited accuracy, while methods offering better solutions require much more computation.
sources.cited_for: Known methods face a trade-off between speed and solution quality.
sources.not_established: The review gives no efficient classical method for recovering secrets at real cryptographic settings.

sources.showed: Chen reported a bug and withdrew his claim of an efficient quantum algorithm for recovering secrets from noisy equations with a particular relationship between their numerical range and error size.

sources.cited_for: A claimed quantum advance lost its central running-time claim after a bug was found.
sources.not_established: The withdrawn claim establishes no working attack on ML-KEM or efficient classical solution.

shown: The methods reviewed by Alice Pellet-Mary illustrate the remaining obstacle. Algorithms can solve lattice problems quickly with loose accuracy guarantees, or spend much more computation obtaining better answers. Neither capability establishes efficient secret recovery at cryptographic settings.
missing: A correct classical algorithm with a proved polynomial running time for a growing family of cryptographically relevant problems remains to be demonstrated.
Repeated recovery of shared secrets from public information at unchanged ML-KEM-1024 settings remains to be demonstrated.
Independent reproduction with practical computing costs, including memory and preparation, remains to be demonstrated.

milestones.label: A reviewed proof of correctness and efficient scaling
milestones.explanation: A peer-reviewed algorithm would have to prove correctness and polynomial running time for a defined, growing family of relevant problems, including preparation costs. This would establish its mathematical guarantee.

milestones.label: Repeated shared-secret recovery at standard settings
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to recover shared secrets across independently generated, unchanged ML-KEM-1024 cases using public keys and encrypted messages. This would establish success against the practical target.

milestones.label: A reproducible public attack with measured computing costs
milestones.explanation: Released code and experimental details would have to enable independent reproduction using only public inputs, with time, memory, preparation and failures reported. This would establish reproducibility and practical cost.

milestones.label: Demonstrated limits on performance, scaling and broader reach
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to establish performance at ML-KEM-1024, and proofs would have to justify scaling and any broader claims. This would establish which problems and cryptographic systems the method actually reaches.

uncertain: The running-time growth, computing budget and success rate sufficient for practical completion still need justification.
The connection between a general lattice solver’s accuracy and recovery of ML-KEM secrets requires its own mathematical argument or explicit attack.
An attack exploiting ML-KEM’s particular structure could have a narrower reach than a general solution to lattice problems.

page.title: Classical polynomial-time Module-LWE secret recovery
page.definition: A classical algorithm recovers a secret vector of polynomials from noisy linear equations over a fixed polynomial ring. For every module rank k ≥ 4, where k is the number of polynomials in the vector, a fixed power of the input size bounds the growth of the computational cost. At rank four, the same algorithm also recovers the shared secret of an unmodified ML-KEM-1024 exchange from its public encapsulation key and ciphertext.

goal.need: U.S. national security systems specify ML-KEM-1024 for key establishment at every classification level under CNSA 2.0. Hybrid ML-KEM also protected about 70% of browser traffic reaching one large web network in September 2026. A demonstrated weakness at the parameters a system uses would give its operators grounds to switch to a scheme based on a different problem, such as the code-based backup HQC. Faster results on reduced instances alone cannot guide that decision. A hybrid TLS session can remain secure while its elliptic-curve exchange holds.

statements.body: National Institute of Standards and Technology
statements.quote: The security of ML-KEM is related to the computational difficulty of the Module Learning with Errors problem.
We would be very happy to see more cryptanalysis of our challenges, with the goal to foster confidence in PQ parameter selection.
statements.context: The October 24 statement to the NIST post-quantum cryptography forum concerns the team's reduced Kyber parameter sets. It specifies no polynomial-time target.

completion.title: A classical Module-LWE solver has a polynomial bound and breaks unmodified ML-KEM-1024.
completion.criterion: A peer-reviewed classical algorithm recovers s from (A,t=As+e) over R=Z_3329[X]/(X^256+1), for every rank k≥4, with A uniform in R^{k×k} and independent CBD₂ coefficients for s,e∈R^k. Success is at least 1/poly(k), and total bit cost, including preprocessing, is poly(k). CBD₂ is the difference of two sums of two independent unbiased bits. The same algorithm executes shared-key recovery from only an unmodified FIPS 203 ML-KEM-1024 encapsulation key and ciphertext, violating NIST's category-5 security floor.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no outside body located that specifies this joint asymptotic and executed-attack test.
completion.basis: The Atlas fixes the polynomial ring and varies the module rank to give the running-time claim a defined family of inputs. That family uses a uniform public matrix. FIPS 203 fixes the rank of ML-KEM-1024 at four and generates its matrix pseudorandomly from a public seed. The concrete test therefore requires a separate demonstration on the standardized exchange. NIST supplies the category 5 resource comparison.

milestones.title: A classical algorithm recovers a key from a 128-coefficient Bochum Kyber challenge.
milestones.criterion: Recover the secret key of one published Bochum Kyber-128 instance by classical computation using its published parameters. The secret contains n × k = 128 coefficients, where n is the polynomial ring degree and k is the module rank.
milestones.set_by: Bochum Challenges team, secret-key recovery rule and Kyber-128 parameter cards.
milestones.threshold_quote: we consider a parameter set solved when you recover its secret key

milestones.criterion: Recover the secret key of one published Bochum Kyber-256 instance by classical computation using its published parameters. The secret contains n × k = 256 coefficients. Any module rank offered in the Kyber-256 challenge qualifies.
milestones.set_by: Bochum Challenges team, secret-key recovery rule and the Complex category's Kyber-256 parameter cards.
milestones.threshold_quote: we consider a parameter set solved when you recover its secret key

milestones.title: A classical attack on ML-KEM-1024 violates NIST's category-5 security floor.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate classical recovery of the shared secret from only a public encapsulation key and ciphertext produced by unmodified ML-KEM-1024. Show that the resources required fall below NIST's category 5 comparison with AES-256 key search, accounting for success probability, preprocessing and memory on a common cost model.
milestones.set_by: NIST defines the category 5 comparison in section 4.A.5 of its PQC Security Evaluation Criteria. The Atlas requires an executed demonstration using public inputs.
milestones.threshold_quote: must require computational resources comparable to or greater than those required for key search on a block cipher with a 256-bit key
